title: 04 Alternating attention
lines: In frame-wise attention, the stacked tokens have shape 3 by 1374 by 1024, so each image attends only to its own 1374 tokens.
For global attention, we reshape: the three rows are concatenated into one long sequence.
Now every token can attend to every other token, across all three images.
The shape becomes 1 by 4122 by 1024, and 4122 is simply 3 times 1374.
Take the white point's token: it has index 799 in the second image, so its new position is 1 times 1374 plus 799, which is 2173.
tts: In frame-wise attention, the stacked tokens have shape three by thirteen seventy-four by ten twenty-four, so each image attends only to its own thirteen seventy-four tokens.
For global attention, we reshape: the three rows are concatenated into one long sequence.
Now every token can attend to every other token, across all three images.
The shape becomes one by forty-one twenty-two by ten twenty-four, and forty-one twenty-two is simply three times thirteen seventy-four.
Take the white point's token: it has index seven ninety-nine in the second image, so its new position is one times thirteen seventy-four plus seven ninety-nine, which is twenty-one seventy-three.

title: 05 Nine camera numbers
lines: After 24 rounds, the camera head reads out the camera token as nine numbers.
The first four are a quaternion q, which encodes the rotation.
The next three are the translation t, and the last two are the field of view, in radians.
A 60 degree field of view on a 518 pixel image gives a focal length of 259 over tan 30 degrees, which is 448.6 pixels.
tts: After twenty-four rounds, the camera head reads out the camera token as nine numbers.
The first four are a quaternion q, which encodes the rotation.
The next three are the translation t, and the last two are the field of view, in radians.
A sixty degree field of view on a five eighteen pixel image gives a focal length of two fifty-nine over tan thirty degrees, which is four hundred forty-eight point six pixels.

title: 06 Comparing two methods
lines: Route two starts from depth and camera. First, multiply K inverse by u, v, 1 to get the viewing ray of this pixel.
Scale that ray by the depth, 1.975 meters, and we get the point in camera 2's frame.
Then subtract t and multiply by R transpose to move it into camera 1's frame.
In Table 3, this route reaches a Chamfer distance of 0.677, lower than the direct point head at 0.709, and lower is better.
